text: Peyton Farquhar. <break time="0.8s" /> A wealthy planter from an old Alabama family. <break time="0.8s" /> Was a slave owner. <break time="0.8s" /> Who strongly supported. <break time="0.8s" /> The Southern side in the war. <break time="0.8s" /> Unable to join the army. <break time="0.8s" /> For reasons he could not control. <break time="0.8s" /> He longed for a chance. <break time="0.8s" /> To do something brave for the South. <break time="0.8s" /> One evening. <break time="0.8s" /> While Farquhar and his wife. <break time="0.8s" /> Were sitting on a bench near the gate. <break time="0.8s" /> A soldier in a gray uniform. <break time="0.8s" /> Rode up to them. <break time="0.8s" /> Missus Farquhar was glad. <break time="0.8s" /> To bring him a cup of water. <break time="0.8s" /> And while she was gone. <break time="0.8s" /> Her husband eagerly asked. <break time="0.8s" /> For news from the front. <break time="0.8s" /> The soldier said that the Northern army had reached the Owl Creek bridge. <break time="0.8s" /> Where they were repairing the railroad. <break time="0.8s" /> And had built a small fort. <break time="0.8s" /> Any civilian caught. <break time="0.8s" /> Damaging the railroad or its bridges. <break time="0.8s" /> Will be hanged. <break time="0.8s" /> He added. <break time="0.8s" /> And I have seen the order myself. <break time="0.8s" /> Smiling, Farquhar asked. <break time="0.8s" /> What a brave man could do there. <break time="0.8s" /> If he managed to get past the guard. <break time="0.8s" /> At the end of the bridge. <break time="0.8s" /> The soldier answered that a great pile of dry driftwood. <break time="0.8s" /> Lay against the wooden pier. <break time="0.8s" /> And that it would burn very easily. <break time="0.8s" /> Later that night. <break time="0.8s" /> The soldier rode back past the plantation. <break time="0.8s" /> In the opposite direction. <break time="0.8s" /> For he was really. <break time="0.8s" /> A Northern scout in disguise.
